item.title: Intel, Amazon Earnings Spark Tech Selloff as AI Fears Mount
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Tech stocks sold off for a second consecutive day as a rotation out of the AI trade accelerated, after earnings from Amazon and Intel raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Binance has suffered the crypto industry’s biggest-ever hack in a fresh blow to efforts to push digital assets into the mainstream. The exchange said $6.3 billion worth of funds were affected, with $3 billion in crypto frozen, and that it had suspended all withdrawals as it works with law enforcement and completes a security revamp. And France unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, putting the economy on a weak footing as it faces headwinds from surging borrowing costs, violent protests and political and budgetary uncertainty. Today guests: Gonzalo García San Miguel, Abenójar Tungsten, CEO; Sander van ’t Noordende, Randstad, CEO (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: UK Chancellor John Healey Defends Budget Plans
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, the tech rally stalled as Google parent Alphabet slumped 10% post-market on concerns its massive AI spending isn't paying off. Samsung also fell after it withheld its shareholder payout plans until January 2027. The US Federal Reserve held interest rates as policymakers look for more data on the inflation outlook. And the UK Chancellor has told Bloomberg his Budget will tackle the deficit. John Healey unveiled a modest maiden budget, with measures to bring in £6.6 billion in additional revenue by fiscal year 2030-31. Today's guest: Rufaro Chiriseri, RBC Wealth Management, Head of Fixed Income. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: What Wall Street Really Thinks About the AI Trade Now

It has been a big week for the AI trade — we've seen wobbles in the market, many of them in response to headlines like the Anthropic S-1 and earnings from the hyperscalers (Oracle, Microsoft, etc.). So what does Wall Street make of all the news, and how are they processing an increasing sense that the laws of the economy barely apply to AI? Today, we speak with Alexander 'Alty' Altmann, global head of equities tactical strategies at Barclays, and he helps us make sense of how Wall Street really feels about the AI trade right now. We also talk about the KOSPI-fication of the S&P 500, if there are any historical precedents for the capex going into the AI buildout, and if AI is really immune to interest rates. item.description:
After enduring years of crippling power cuts, South Africa’s state utility Eskom has swung to an operational surplus, maintaining 3 to 5 gigawatts of excess generation capacity, according to CEO Dan Marokane. Yet across Johannesburg, localized outages persist as the city works to strengthen its finances and manage its power network. Speaking to Bloomberg’s Jennifer Zabasajja on Next Africa, Marokane discusses the city’s progress on settling overdue electricity bills and plans to ring-fence electricity revenue. He also outlines how Eskom’s recovery is enabling cross-border exports to neighboring southern African states, and explains why reliable electricity is central to rebuilding Johannesburg’s economy. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Odd Lots: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature
item.description:
Regency-era novelist Maria Edgeworth was famous for including economic concepts into her novels, including the idea of productive labor. Her works were ahead of her time and enormously influential, yet her name is hardly ever mentioned in the history of economics. On this episode of the Odd Lots podcast, Jeanna Smialek, Brussels bureau chief at The New York Times, tells Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway why she thinks Edgeworth's name needs to be placed back in the pantheon of economic history. (Source: Bloomberg)

Power cuts, water shortages and crumbling roads are undermining Johannesburg’s economy and threatening its ability to retain businesses and attract investment. Can South Africa’s City of Gold turn itself around? On this episode of Next Africa, Jennifer Zabasajja examines the financial pressures and political instability behind Johannesburg’s decline, and whether upcoming local elections could help change its course. Business Leadership South Africa CEO Busi Mavuso explains why companies are being forced to work around failing public services. Ninety One founder and CEO Hendrik du Toit discusses the investment needed to rebuild the city, while Eskom CEO Dan Marokane explains how the utility moved from rolling blackouts to excess generating capacity—and why Johannesburg still faces outages. Plus, Bloomberg South Africa Bureau Chief Alex Parker assesses the city’s infrastructure backlog and prospects for recovery. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods
item.description:
It's obvious that things are getting more expensive, and there are plenty of reasons behind the surge in prices — whether it's wars or inflation or companies padding their profit margins. But with the release of AI agents like Meta's Muse, tech companies are promising consumers that agents will start saving them tons of money by finding the best deals. According to today's guest, Lindsay Owens, the history of price gouging does not bode well for claims that things might get cheaper because of new technology, and research conducted by her think tank Groundwork Collaborative shows that a number of consumer facing agents end up serving customers more expensive items after learning more about their financial situation. Her new book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — and What That Means for Your Wallet gets into the history of how companies got away with charging more for their goods, through means like data collection and surveillance. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Bloomberg

item.title: The Forgotten Godmother of Economic Literature
item.description:
In 1776, the field of economics was born with the publication of Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations. Among the book's earliest readers was a Regency-era novelist named Maria Edgeworth. In her time, Edgeworth was one of the most famous literary figures in England, and she smuggled into her stories economic concepts and debates around rent seeking, the idea of productive labor, and so on. These works were enormously influential and they helped expose a generation to practical applications of Smith's theories. Jeanna Smialek, a veteran Fed reporter and the Brussels bureau chief at The New York Times, thinks Edgeworth's name needs to be placed back in the pantheon of economic history. Today, we discuss Edgeworth's friendly debates with the likes of Thomas Malthus and David Ricardo, how the Irish potato famine reshaped economic thought, and how Edgeworth used the novel form to educate the masses on the value of economics. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Olivia Solon, Tom Mackenzie and Christina Kyriasoglou

item.title: Bhaskar Sunkara Thinks the Market Has a Place Under Socialism
item.description:
In September, Gallup released a poll that showed that 43% percent of Americans viewed socialism positively, the highest approval since Gallup began the poll back in 2010. Since Zohran Mamdani won the NYC mayoral election, the left has made a number of gains across national politics. As a longtime DSA member and veteran of leftist media, Bhaskar Sunkara is one of socialism's leading advocates, and he's spent much of his career charting what a socialist economy in America might look like. Unlike some other leftists, he believes the market has a place. In fact, he thinks markets and entrepreneurs are an objective good in society. He proposes a vision of so-called "market socialism" in his recent co-authored book The Blueprint, and he lays out this system for us in today's episode. We talk about how many features of capitalism — from small businesses to monetary policy — might be remade under socialist principles. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Berlin, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, global stocks fell after a mixed start to US tech earnings failed to calm nerves around the AI trade. Meta doubled down on its investment plans, boosting its capital spending forecast for the year. Oil advanced after deadly Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia. Two people were killed in a drone strike on an Aramco oil field and one person died in an attack on an airport. The US has ordered non-emergency personnel and their families to leave the country. item.author: Natalia Ojewska

item.title: James Robinson on What It Looks Like When a State is Failing
item.description:
The third and last episode from our Chicago live show is with James Robinson, a professor at the University of Chicago and a recipient of the 2024 Nobel Prize in economics (which he shared with Daron Acemoglu and Simon Johnson). His most famous work is 2012's Why Nations Fail, and in that book he and his co-author Acemoglu document the institutional factors — whether it is reliably run elections or open markets that help facilitate innovation — that determine why some states thrive and others don't. So we ask Robinson the big question: What would have to happen for the US to be considered a failed state? (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Musk Calls for SpaceX-Tesla Mega Merger
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Berlin, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, global stocks gained as strong tech earnings eased concerns over the AI trade. SpaceX reported blowout third-quarter results with net income of $4.4 billion soaring past the average estimate of $1.88 billion. CEO Elon Musk seized on the momentum to call for a mega-merger with Tesla. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is due to speak at the company's GTC developer conference in Berlin. Today's guests: Lars-Hendrik Röller, Berlin Global Dialogue, Founder; Maria Ferraro, Siemens Energy, CFO; Martin Blessing, German Chancellor's Special Representative for Investments in Germany; Christian Sewing, Deutsche Bank, CEO. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Alice Atkins

item.title: CME's Terry Duffy on the Disconcerting State of Finance Regulation
item.description:
The CFTC was practically brand new when Terry Duffy started working at the CME almost five decades ago, and over the course of his career at the exchange, this legend of the trading world has seen an enormous amount of change when it comes to finance regulation, including the rise of prediction markets, 24/7 trading and perpetual futures. Duffy is set to transition out of his current position as CME CEO next year, and this conversation, recorded live at City Winery in Chicago, is a sort of exit interview. He tells us how regulation has evolved since the start of his time at the CME. We also talk about why he is against perps, the credibility issues prediction markets face, his definition of spreads versus futures, and what he wishes he knew at the start of his career now that he is nearing retirement. (Source: Bloomberg)

Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, AI jitters returned after the Korean data center firm Elice flopped on its stock market debut. Shares fell as much as 35% after its IPO, which raised $151 million. Bloomberg has learnt that the AI cloud computing firm Nscale is in talks to sell computing power to Anthropic, in a deal that could be worth about $45 billion. And tougher security measures, including an 11pm curfew in some parts of Paris and other cities, appear to have quelled violent protests in France for now. A year's time in the age of AI is an eternity, and so for the first episode of this year's Chicago live show - recorded at City Winery - Wilson joins us on stage again to talk about what's changed and what hasn't in his quest to help build this market. We get his take on the recent tech selloff, including credit concerns around neocloud CoreWeave. item.author: Sara Gharaibeh

item.title: David Byrne Explains How Forgotten Ideas Come Back to Life
item.description:
History is littered with ideas that have been tossed aside, only for them to gain relevance at some later date. Think of Moby-Dick: forgotten in Melville's time, but now regarded as the great American novel. Or the work of economist Hyman Minsky, which became influential a decade after his death, when the 2008 financial crisis made “the Minsky Moment” a mainstream term. These are just a couple of the things we talk about with the legendary musician David Byrne on today's podcast. Byrne's new book, Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up, looks to categorize numerous “sleeping beauties” — ideas that were lost but then rediscovered. Besides Melville and Minsky, we also talk about the lost Roman recipe for concrete and we get into Byrne's thoughts on how to write a song and his own experience of having his music rediscovered by a new generation. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The French Political Crisis Turning Into a Debt Crisis
item.description:
Just about everyone is worried about what is going on in France right now: the country's public finances are in sorry shape and there are fears that the French bond selloff, and the country's growing debt crisis, might spillover into the rest of Europe. The 2027 elections have investors worried: Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon aren't seen to be up to the task of taming France's fiscal turmoil. Shahin Vallée was an advisor to Emmanuel Macron when he was an economic minister and during his first presidential election campaign. He is currently a senior fellow at the German Council of Foreign Relations and advises institutional investors — and he understands what went wrong during Macron's nine years in office. Today, he speaks to us about the origins of the current French debt crisis, how similar it is to the challenges Greece faced during the first euro crisis, and why the 2027 elections are making an unstable situation even worse. item.title: UK's Healey Plans to Raise Bank Taxes
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. On today's show, global stocks bounced back as dip buyers stepped in after the chip selloff. The European Union is preparing to create new trade powers that could completely shut off access to its single market as part of a dramatic new push to cut the trade deficit with China. And UK Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to raise taxes on banks to fund cost-of-living support for voters and stabilize the public finances, as he looks for sources of revenue that won’t violate Labour Party campaign pledges. item.title: Anthropic Urged to Pause IPO for AI Safety by NYC Comptroller
item.description:

Ed Ludlow reports on Bloomberg Television. (Source: Bloomberg)
